figures.title: Chapter map
figures.why: one flow - identify the frame and forces, then F=ma per body
figures.read: every result is a free-body diagram plus the second law in a chosen frame

figures.title: The three laws: one chain of meaning
figures.why: the laws are a discipline - frame, then force, then the pair
figures.data: First law defines inertial frames; second F=dp/dt; third pairs across bodies
figures.read: frame, then equations, then pair forces across bodies - never on one diagram

figures.title: The FBD protocol: isolate, draw, resolve, solve
figures.why: every mechanics problem is the same five steps
figures.data: incline block: mg down, N perpendicular, f up; mg sinθ / mg cosθ
figures.read: isolation kills the reaction confusion; axes along acceleration decouple

figures.title: Apparent weight: the scale reads the normal force
figures.why: weight in a lift is a normal-force question, not a gravity question
figures.data: rest N=mg, up N=m(g+a), down N=m(g-a), free fall N=0
figures.read: the weight never changed; the reading did

figures.title: Friction is a range, then a plateau
figures.why: static friction grows to a cap, then collapses to the lower kinetic value
figures.data: below cap f=F; peak μsN; plateau μkN < μsN
figures.read: before the cap friction mirrors the push; after it, friction is the smaller constant

figures.title: Triage - route by the keyword
figures.why: the keyword names the route before any number is touched
figures.read: incline words resolve the weight, pulley words differentiate the string, circular words sum toward the centre

drawings.title: Inertial and accelerating frames
drawings.show: left: a ball sitting on a frictionless table in a stationary room — it stays put (inertial frame, first law holds). Right: the same ball in a car that brakes suddenly — the ball appears to slide forward (non-inertial frame, first law appears violated unless a pseudo force is included).
drawings.search: "inertial versus non-inertial frame ball sliding car braking"

drawings.title: Newton's third-law pairs
drawings.show: a block on a table. Force pair 1: Earth pulls block down (weight $mg$), block pulls Earth up ($mg$). Force pair 2: table pushes block up (normal $N$), block pushes table down ($N$). Each pair drawn with equal-length arrows on the two bodies.
drawings.search: "Newton third law action reaction pairs block on table diagram"

drawings.title: Incline free-body diagram and components
drawings.show: left: the physical setup — a block on a ramp inclined at angle $\theta$. Right: the FBD — the block isolated, with weight $mg$ pointing vertically down, normal $N$ perpendicular to the surface, friction $f$ up the incline. Axes: $x$ along the incline (downhill), $y$ perpendicular to the incline. Components: $mg\sin\theta$ along $x$, $mg\cos\theta$ along $y$.
drawings.search: "free body diagram block inclined plane components axes"

drawings.title: Apparent weight in an elevator
drawings.show: a person standing on a scale in a lift. Three cases: (a) lift at rest — scale reads $mg$; (b) lift accelerating up at $a$ — scale reads $m(g+a)$; (c) lift in free fall — scale reads 0 (weightlessness). The FBD for each case with the normal force and weight drawn.
drawings.search: "apparent weight lift accelerating upward downward free fall scale"

drawings.title: Static and kinetic friction graph
drawings.show: a graph of friction $f$ vs applied horizontal force $F$ on a block. For $F<F_{\max}$: $f=F$ (static friction adjusts). At $F=\mu_s N$: the block slips, friction drops to $\mu_k N$ (kinetic regime, roughly constant). The peak is at $\mu_s N$, the plateau at $\mu_k N$.
drawings.search: "friction force versus applied force graph static kinetic peak plateau"

drawings.title: Two blocks and the no-slip limit
drawings.show: two blocks ($m$ on top of $M$) on a frictionless table, pushed by force $F$ on $M$. The friction between the blocks provides the top block's acceleration. If $F$ is too large, the top block slips backward relative to $M$. The critical force $F_{\max}=(M+m)\mu_s g$ annotated.
drawings.search: "stacked blocks maximum force before slipping friction diagram"

drawings.title: Wedge and block displacement constraint
drawings.show: a wedge of angle $\theta$ sliding rightward on a table; a block sliding down the wedge. The block's displacement relative to the wedge is along the incline (length $s$). The wedge's displacement is horizontal ($x_w$). Take the incline to slope downward to the right; the block slides down-right relative to the wedge by $s$, while the wedge moves right by $x_w$. The block's ground-frame displacement is $(x_w+s\cos\theta, -s\sin\theta)$, so its horizontal shift is $x_w+s\cos\theta$ and its vertical drop is $s\sin\theta$. The block remains on the incline.
drawings.search: "wedge block constraint displacement triangle geometry diagram"

drawings.title: Forces at four positions in a vertical circle
drawings.show: a vertical circle with the particle at four positions: bottom (0°), side (90°), top (180°), and an intermediate angle $\theta$. At each: the tension $T$ (toward centre), weight $mg$ (downward), and the centripetal direction shown. At the top: $T$ and $mg$ both point toward the centre. At the bottom: $T$ points up, $mg$ points down.
drawings.search: "vertical circle four positions tension weight centripetal direction"

drawings.title: Two-pulley string constraint
drawings.show: a fixed pulley at the ceiling and a movable pulley below it, connected by a single string. Mass $m_1$ is attached to the movable pulley and mass $m_2$ hangs from the free end after the string passes over the ceiling-fixed pulley. With downward coordinates $x_1$ for the movable pulley and $x_2$ for the free end, $l=2x_1+x_2+\mathrm{const}$. Thus $a_2=-2a_1$ when both downward directions are positive; the free end has twice the acceleration magnitude.
drawings.search: "two pulley single string system constraint acceleration diagram"

drawings.title: Movable-pulley constraint
drawings.show: one end of a light inextensible string is fixed overhead; the string passes down around a movable pulley carrying mass $m_2$, then up over a fixed pulley and down to a free end carrying mass $m_1$. Choose downward coordinates $x_1$ for the free end and $x_2$ for the movable pulley. The variable string length is $x_1+2x_2$, so $x_1+2x_2=\text{constant}$ and hence $a_1=-2a_2$ (signed); the free end's acceleration magnitude is twice the movable pulley's.
drawings.search: "movable pulley string constraint acceleration relation diagram"

drawings.title: Friction on a banked road
drawings.show: a car on a banked curve of angle $\theta$. Left (maximum speed): friction $f$ acts inward (down the incline). The FBD shows $N$, $mg$, $f$ and the centripetal direction. Right (minimum speed): friction acts outward (up the incline). The two speed limits annotated: $v_{\max}$ and $v_{\min}$.
drawings.search: "banked road friction maximum minimum speed both limits diagram"

drawings.title: Vertical-circle tension and speed
drawings.show: left: a graph of tension $T$ vs angle $\theta$ (0 at bottom, minimum near the top, maximum at the bottom). Right: a graph of speed $v$ vs $\theta$ (maximum at the bottom, minimum at the top). The minimum speed at the top $\sqrt{gR}$ annotated. The string-slack angle $\theta_0$ marked.
drawings.search: "vertical circle tension versus angle speed versus angle graph"
